title: Module Overview: From Classical to Generalized Ballot Problem
content:
The module docstring establishes the generalized ballot problem for $k$-fold dominance and outlines the proof strategy via the Dvoretzky-Motzkin cycle lemma. Imports `Archive.Wiedijk100Theorems.BallotProblem` (Mathlib's classical ballot formalization, Wiedijk #30) and `Mathlib.Tactic` for proof automation. Opens `List` and `Set` namespaces for convenient list manipulation.

The generalization from $k=1$ (classical: A always leads B) to arbitrary $k$ (A always has $>k$ times B's votes) changes the lattice path model: downsteps become $-k$ instead of $-1$, making the path analysis significantly harder. The cycle lemma handles this elegantly via rotational symmetry.
mathContext: Classical ($k=1$): $P(\text{A leads throughout}) = \frac{p-q}{p+q}$ (Bertrand 1887). Generalized: $P = \frac{a-kb}{a+b}$ (Dvoretzky-Motzkin 1947). The lattice path has steps $+1$ (A-vote) and $-k$ (B-vote), total displacement $S = a - kb$, and the cycle lemma counts exactly $S$ good rotations out of $n = a+b$.

title: Generalized Ballot Sequences
content:
**kCountedSequence** defines the set of vote sequences for the k-fold ballot problem:
- Exactly `a` votes for candidate A (value +1)
- Exactly `b` votes for candidate B (value $-k$)
- All elements are either 1 or $-k$

The companion **kStaysPositive** captures sequences where all prefix sums are strictly positive, modelling the condition that A leads throughout counting.

When $k = 1$, this is exactly Mathlib's `countedSequence`.
mathContext: $$\text{kCountedSequence}(k,a,b) = \{l \mid l.\text{count}(1) = a \wedge l.\text{count}(-k) = b \wedge \forall x \in l,\, x = 1 \vee x = -k\}$$

title: Sum and Length Identities for Binary Lists
content: For any list with only $1$ and $-k$ values, the sum equals $\text{count}(1) - k \cdot \text{count}(-k)$ and the length equals $\text{count}(1) + \text{count}(-k)$. These are proved by induction on the list, using `List.count_cons` to track how counts change at each step. The sum identity is the algebraic backbone of the ballot theorem: it connects the path's total displacement to the vote counts.

title: Permutation Characterization and Finiteness
content:
Every element of kCountedSequence is a permutation of the canonical witness `replicate a 1 ++ replicate b (-k)`. This is proved using `List.perm_iff_count` — two lists are permutations iff they have the same count for every element. The proof handles three cases: $x = 1$ (use $h_1$), $x = -k$ (use $h_2$), and $x \notin \{1, -k\}$ (both counts are zero).

This characterization immediately gives **finiteness**: the set of permutations of a finite list is finite, so `kCountedSequence` inherits `Set.Finite`.

title: Classical Reduction (k = 1)
content:
When $k = 1$, our generalized definition exactly matches Mathlib's `Ballot.countedSequence`. The proof is remarkably clean: just `simpa` to convert $-(1 : \mathbb{Z})$ to $-1$.

This validates our generalization against the established formalization and ensures backward compatibility with Wiedijk theorem #30.

title: The Generalized Ballot Theorem Statement
content: The main theorem statements: `generalized_ballot_count` asserts the counting formula via double counting (still has 1 sorry), while `generalized_ballot_prob` proves the probability $(a - kb)/(a + b) > 0$ when $a > kb$. Verified special cases include $(5, 2, 2) \to 1/7$, $(10, 3, 3) \to 1/13$, $(3, 1, 1) \to 1/2$, and $(7, 2, 3) \to 1/10$.
mathContext: $$P(\text{A leads throughout}) = \frac{a - kb}{a + b} > 0 \quad \text{when } a > kb$$

title: Cyclic Rotation and Membership Preservation
content:
Defines cyclic rotation as $\text{rotate}(l, i) = \text{drop}\,i\,l \mathbin{\|}\, \text{take}\,i\,l$ and proves key invariants: rotation preserves the sum ($\sum \text{rotate}(l,i) = \sum l$), the length, and membership in kCountedSequence. The membership proof uses `List.take_append_drop` to show that counts are additive over the split.

Composition of rotations satisfies $\text{rotate}(\text{rotate}(l, i), j) = \text{rotate}(l, i+j)$ when indices don't exceed the boundary.

title: Prefix Sum Relation for Rotations
content:
The key structural lemma for the cycle lemma. For rotation starting at position $i$, the prefix sum at position $j$ decomposes into two cases depending on whether $i + j$ wraps around. The non-wrapping case uses `take_drop_sum`, while the wrapping case involves `List.take_append` and a careful re-indexing via `List.take_take`.

This lemma is the technical heart of the file — it connects the combinatorial structure of rotations to the analytic property of prefix sums.

title: Good Rotations and Decidability
content:
A rotation is **good** if all prefix sums of the rotated sequence are strictly positive — equivalently, if the corresponding vote counting always has A leading with more than $k$ times B's votes. The `isGoodRotation` predicate is made `Decidable` by reducing to a finite conjunction over $j \in [1, n]$, enabling `native_decide` verification of concrete examples.

`goodRotations l` collects all good starting positions as a `Finset ℕ`.

title: Rightmost Minimum Infrastructure
content:
Defines `rightmostMinPos l` as the **rightmost** position where the prefix sum achieves its global minimum, and proves it is a good rotation when $S > 0$. The key insight: after the rightmost minimum, all prefix sums are strictly above the minimum (by maximality), so the non-wrapping part of the rotated prefix sums is positive. The wrapping part uses $\sigma(j) \geq \min + 0$ and the positive sum $S > 0$ to stay positive.

This gives the existence of at least one good rotation, which is needed to start the counting argument.
mathContext: $$m = \max\{i \leq n : \sigma(i) = \min_{0 \leq j \leq n} \sigma(j)\}, \qquad \text{rotation } m \text{ is good}$$

title: Cycle Lemma Upper Bound via Injection
content: Proves $|\text{goodRotations}| \leq S$ by constructing an **injection** from good rotations into $\{0, 1, \ldots, S-1\}$. The injection maps each good rotation $i$ to $(\sigma(i) - \min)$, which lies in $[0, S)$ by the prefix sum bounds. Injectivity follows from `goodRotation_prefixSum_injective`: if two good rotations have equal prefix sums, they must be equal (since prefix sums are strictly monotone on good rotations).

title: Discrete Intermediate Value Theorem for Prefix Sums
content:
Proves that for every integer level $v \in [\min(\sigma), \min(\sigma) + S)$, there exists a position $i < n$ with $\sigma(i) = v$. The proof uses `Finset.max'` to find the rightmost position $j$ with $\sigma(j) \leq v$. By maximality, $\sigma(j+1) > v$. Since the only way to increase is by $+1$ steps, the element at position $j$ must be $+1$, forcing $\sigma(j) = v$ exactly.

This is a discrete analogue of the intermediate value theorem, exploiting the $+1$ step structure.

title: Cycle Lemma Lower Bound via levelPos Surjection
content: `goodRotations_card_ge` proves $|\text{goodRotations}| \geq a - kb$ by constructing a surjection from $\{0, \ldots, a-kb-1\}$ into `goodRotations` via `levelPos`. For each integer level $n < a-kb$, `levelPos l n` is the rightmost position where the prefix sum is $\leq \min(\sigma) + n$. The key theorem `levelPos_eq` (lines 703-725) proves that `prefixSum l (levelPos l n) = minPrefixSum l + n` exactly, by showing that the step at `levelPos` must be $+1$ (if it were $-k$, the next prefix sum would be too low, contradicting maximality). Injectivity of `levelPos` follows: if $\text{levelPos}(n_1) = \text{levelPos}(n_2)$, then $\min(\sigma) + n_1 = \min(\sigma) + n_2$, so $n_1 = n_2$.
mathContext:
$$g(n) = \text{levelPos}(l, n), \quad g : \{0, \ldots, S-1\} \hookrightarrow \text{goodRotations}$$

Each $g(n)$ is the rightmost position where $\sigma \leq \min(\sigma) + n$. The $+1$ step structure forces $\sigma(g(n)) = \min(\sigma) + n$ exactly, making $g$ injective.

title: native_decide Verification Examples
content: Three concrete examples verified by `native_decide`: $[1,1,-1]$ has 1 good rotation (out of 3), $[1,1,1,-1,-1]$ has 1 (out of 5), and $[1,1,1,-1]$ has 2 (out of 4). These match the cycle lemma formula: $a - kb$ gives $2-1=1$, $3-2=1$, and $3-1=2$ respectively. The `native_decide` tactic evaluates the decidable predicate `isGoodRotation` for each rotation, providing brute-force verification independent of the cycle lemma proof.

title: The Cycle Lemma (Dvoretzky-Motzkin, 1947)
content:
**The main result**: for a ballot sequence $l \in \text{kCountedSequence}(k,a,b)$ with $a > kb$, exactly $a - kb$ of the $a + b$ cyclic rotations have all positive prefix sums. The proof combines the upper bound (injection into $\{0, \ldots, S-1\}$) and the lower bound (surjection from $\{0, \ldots, S-1\}$ via `levelPos`) into the equality $|\text{goodRotations}| = S = a - kb$.

This resolves the key counting problem originally posed by Dvoretzky and Motzkin in 1947.
mathContext: $$|\text{goodRotations}(l)| = a - kb \qquad \text{for } l \in \text{kCountedSequence}(k, a, b),\; a > kb$$

title: Lattice Path Interpretation: Geometry of Vote Counting
content:
The concluding section provides the geometric interpretation that unifies the entire formalization. Each vote sequence maps to a lattice path: A-votes are $+1$ upsteps and B-votes are $-k$ downsteps. The ballot condition (A always has $>k$ times B's votes) corresponds to the path staying strictly above the $x$-axis. The cycle lemma counts exactly $a - kb$ favorable starting positions out of $a + b$ total rotations, giving the probability $P = (a-kb)/(a+b)$.

This geometric viewpoint connects the ballot problem to a rich tradition in combinatorics: Dyck paths ($k=1$, counted by Catalan numbers), Motzkin paths (with horizontal steps), and general lattice paths with prescribed step sets. The $k$-fold generalization studied here corresponds to paths with the asymmetric step set $\{+1, -k\}$.
mathContext: The lattice path $(x_0, y_0), (x_1, y_1), \ldots, (x_n, y_n)$ with $x_i = i$ and $y_i = \sigma(i) = \sum_{j=1}^{i} l_j$ stays above the $x$-axis iff $\sigma(i) > 0$ for all $1 \leq i \leq n$. For $k=1$: these are Dyck paths, counted by $C_n = \frac{1}{n+1}\binom{2n}{n}$. For general $k$: the paths have the asymmetric step set $\{+1, -k\}$ and are counted by the cycle lemma.
